Q1

```{r}
f<- function(th){
  p<-(3*th^2-1)/(1+th^3)
  return(p)
}

#First derivative
fp<- function(th){
  p<-(6*th-3*th^4+3*th^2)/(1+th^3)^2
  return(p)
}

#Second derivative
fpp <- function(th){
  p<-6*(th^6-2*th^2-7*th^3+th+1)/(1+th^3)^3
  return(p)
}

#Newton Method 
diff<- 4
iter<- 0
th<-1.5
while((diff>0.001)&&(iter<30)){
  oldth<-th
  th<-th-fp(th)/fpp(th)
  diff<- abs(th-oldth)
  iter<-iter+1
  print(c(iter,diff))
}
th


```
The maximizer is theta = 1.52163

Q2 (a)
```{r}
sales <- c(61,73,85,106,120,129,142,144,161)
ad <- c(19,26,30,34,43,48,52,57,68)
X <- cbind(1,ad)
Y <- as.matrix(sales)
I <-diag(2)

#Ridge regression with lambda
#1. lambda =0.1

lambda <- 0.1
theta_ridge1 <- solve(t(X)%*%X + lambda*I)%*%t(X)%*%Y
theta_ridge1

#2. lambda = 1

lambda <- 1
theta_ridge2 <- solve(t(X)%*%X + lambda*I)%*%t(X)%*%Y
theta_ridge2


#3. lambda = 10

lambda <- 10
theta_ridge3 <- solve(t(X)%*%X + lambda*I)%*%t(X)%*%Y
theta_ridge3


#4. lambda = 100

lambda <- 100
theta_ridge4 <- solve(t(X)%*%X + lambda*I)%*%t(X)%*%Y
theta_ridge4






```

(b) As lambda increases in ridge regression the intercept decreases susbtantially and the slope increases slightly. The ridge regression shrinks coefficients but never becomes equal to 0. Ridge uses an L2 penalty whose constraint is a circle. Since a circle does not have any sharp corners the solution rarely lands exactly on zero. 
LASSO uses L1 penalty whose constraint is a diamond (tighter constraint), it has sharp corners so the solution often lands exactly at zero. LASSO produces sparse solutions.
Therefore, ridge keeps all predictors in the model while LASSO eliminates some predictors producing a sparse model. 



Q3 (a)
```{r}
german <- read.table("german.data", header = FALSE)

german$default <- ifelse(german$V21 == 2, 1, 0)

factor_vars <- c(1,3,4,6,7,9,10,12,14,15,17,19,20)
german[factor_vars] <- lapply(german[factor_vars], factor)

set.seed(060720)
train_index <- sample(1:1000, 900)


train <- german[train_index, ]
test  <- german[-train_index, ]

model1 <- glm(default ~ V2 + V5 + V13 + V1, data = train, family = binomial )

summary(model1)
```
To interpret the regression coefficient, we pick V2 with coefficient = 0.03349
```{r}
exp(0.03349)
```
```{r}
prob1 <- predict(model1, newdata = test, type = "response")
head(prob1)
```
Cutoff chosen = 0.5
```{r}
cutoff <- 0.5
pred1 <- ifelse(prob1 >= cutoff, 1, 0)
```

Create a confusion matrix:-
```{r}
cm1 <- table(actual= test$default, predicted= pred1)
cm1
```

Setting labels for the entries in the confusion matrix:-
```{r}
FN1 <- cm1["1","0"] #FN=False Negative
FP1 <- cm1["0","1"] #FP=False Positive
TN1 <- cm1["1","1"] #TN=True Negative
TP1 <- cm1["0","0"] #TP=True Positive

FN1
FP1

err1 <- FN1 + FP1
err1
```
11 default ones were predicted to be non-default and 8 non-default ones were predicted to be default ones. 



Adding more predictors and interaction term between V2(Loan duration) and V5 (Credit amount) for model 2 :-
```{r}
model2 <- glm(default ~ V2 + V5 + V13 + V8 + V1 + V3 + V4 + V7 +  V2:V5, data = train, family = binomial)
summary(model2)
```

Now we predict and classify the errors for model 2 with cut off =0.5
```{r}
prob2 <- predict(model2, newdata = test, type="response")
pred2 <- ifelse(prob2 >= cutoff, 1, 0)

cm2 <- table(actual=test$default, predicted=pred2)
cm2

FN2 <- cm2["1","0"] #FN=False Negative
FP2 <- cm2["0","1"] #FP=False Positive
TN2 <- cm2["1","1"] #TN=True Negative
TP2 <- cm2["0","0"] #TP=True Positive

FN2
FP2

err2 <- FN2 + FP2
err2

```
13<19
Error in model 2 < error from model 1

(b) Computing Sensitivity and specificity across different cutoffs:-

```{r}
# At cutoff = 0.2
cutoff <- 0.2
pred_02 <- ifelse(prob2 >= cutoff, 1, 0)

cm_02 <- table(test$default, pred_02)
cm_02

TN_02 <- cm_02["0","0"]
FP_02 <- cm_02["0","1"]
FN_02 <- cm_02["1","0"]
TP_02 <- cm_02["1","1"]

sens_02 <- TP_02/(TP_02+FN_02) #sensitivity
spec_02 <- TN_02/(TN_02+FP_02) #specificity

sens_02
spec_02

```
At 0.2 cutoff (low) - most applicants are rejected, therefore, specificity decreases.

```{r}
# At cutoff = 0.45
cutoff <- 0.45
pred_45 <- ifelse(prob2 >= cutoff, 1, 0)

cm_45 <- table(test$default, pred_45)
cm_45

TN_45 <- cm_45["0","0"]
FP_45 <- cm_45["0","1"]
FN_45 <- cm_45["1","0"]
TP_45 <- cm_45["1","1"]

sens_45 <- TP_45/(TP_45+FN_45) #sensitivity
spec_45 <- TN_45/(TN_45+FP_45) #specificity

sens_45
spec_45
```
At cutoff = 0.45 we see more applicants getting accepted and specificity increases.

```{r}
# At cutoff = 0.7
cutoff <- 0.7
pred_7 <- ifelse(prob2 >= cutoff, 1, 0)

cm_7 <- table(test$default, pred_7)
cm_7

TN_7 <- cm_7["0","0"]
FP_7 <- cm_7["0","1"]
FN_7 <- cm_7["1","0"]
TP_7 <- cm_7["1","1"]

sens_7 <- TP_7/(TP_7+FN_7) #sensitivity
spec_7 <- TN_7/(TN_7+FP_7) #specificity

sens_7
spec_7
```
At cut off =0.7 almost everyone gets accepted the specificity increases to 0.98 and sensitivity drops to 0.4
Therefore, as the cutoff probability increases, sensitivity decreases while specificity increases. Higher cutoffs reduce false positives but miss more defaulters/risky customers.
